pages.text:
Here is what you need to know about my little brother Gus: he had not taken off his T. rex costume in forty-one days.

Not for baths (he sat in the tub in it, like a wet green sofa). Not for picture day. Not for the dentist, who said "Open wide" and got a roar in the face.

So when I tell you that at 6:47 on the morning of the worst day of my life a dinosaur climbed onto my chest and screamed, you should not be surprised. You should be asking a different question, which is: why did I wake up already feeling like a person who had lost?

"RAAAAWR," said the dinosaur, with his whole face an inch from mine.

"I'm awake," I said.

"RAAAAWR."

"Gus, I'm awake. We're both awake. That's the only thing that's going right."

He sat back on my ribs, pleased, and the spikes on his tail knocked over the water glass on my floor. Nobody had packed the water glass. It was the last thing in my room that nobody had packed.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy with messy hair, lies flat in a bare bed looking doomed while Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, sits on his chest with his mouth wide open, roaring; morning light, cardboard boxes in the corner.

pages.text:
I should explain about the room.

Yesterday it had been a room. It had a desk with a lamp shaped like a rocket, a bookshelf, a beanbag that was mostly beans, and a wall of posters that I'd stuck up one at a time over six years. Now the walls were bare except for pale rectangles where the posters had been, like the marks a sunburn leaves after a strap comes off. My bed was the only furniture left. Next to it sat one cardboard box with MAX'S STUFF (MISC.) printed on the side in Mom's tidy capitals.

I knew what MISC. meant. It meant: things Max won't throw away and won't look at either.

Dunmore, Ohio, is the only place I have ever lived. I know which stair on our porch creaks. I know which streetlight on Larkspur Lane flickers when it's about to rain. I know that you can hear the ice-cream truck two full minutes before it turns the corner, which gives you time to find a dollar.

Tomorrow morning a moving truck was going to arrive at seven o'clock sharp, and by tomorrow night we would be living in Tucson, Arizona, which is 1,700 miles away. I looked it up. I looked it up three times, hoping it would change. It's mostly cactus.
pages.image: Max sits on the edge of a bare bed in an empty bedroom, looking at pale rectangles on the walls where posters used to be, one lonely cardboard box on the floor beside him; grey morning light.

pages.text:
At 7:13, Waffles stole my left slipper.

Waffles is our dog. He's a corgi, which means he has the body of a loaf of bread and the morals of a pirate. He trotted past my door with the slipper hanging out of his mouth like a cigar, gave me a look that said *come and get me*, and vanished under the dining room table, which I could see from the hall because there was nothing left in the house to block the view.

I crawled after him. Under the table were: one lost sock, one red Lego brick, and a french fry so old it had turned into a fossil. Waffles lay in the middle of them, chewing my slipper with the expression of a dog who has never had a single regret.

"Roar at someone else," I said, because Gus was right behind me, growling down at my ankles.

That was all I said. I didn't even say it loudly.

But Gus stopped. I watched his face go small inside the dinosaur hood, the way a kid's face does when he has just realized the game was only his. He sat down on the floor with his tail sticking out behind him.

I noticed. I want that on the record. I noticed, and then I picked up my slipper and pretended I hadn't.
pages.image: Max on hands and knees peers under a dining table where Waffles, a chubby corgi, chews a slipper next to a lost sock, a red Lego and a fossilized french fry; behind Max, Gus in a green T. rex costume sits on the floor looking small and sad.

pages.text:
At 7:22 the smoke alarm went off.

This was not news. Dad burns the toast every single morning. He believes the toaster is broken and the toaster believes Dad is broken, and neither one has ever been willing to see a specialist.

When I walked into the kitchen he was standing on a chair in his apron (the one with the cartoon fish on it), fanning the ceiling with a dish towel and shouting over the beeping.

"Max! Good morning! Did you know I'm reading a book about anti-gravity?"

"No."

"It's impossible to put down!"

He waited. His mustache was up, hopeful. My dad has a face like a big friendly loaf, and when he makes a pun it lights up like he has just handed you a present.

I did not laugh. I had decided in bed that I wasn't going to laugh at anything today, on principle, and the principle was going great.

Mom went by in the doorway with her clipboard. Six pages, stapled. A pencil behind her ear and another one in her mouth. She ticked something off without looking up.

"Sal," she said around the pencil, "the toast."

"It's not burnt, Mira," said Dad. "It's *dark.*"
pages.image: Dad, a big round man with a dark mustache in a fish apron, stands on a chair fanning a screaming smoke alarm with a dish towel, smiling hopefully; Max in a red hoodie stands stone-faced in the doorway; Mom with a clipboard hurries past.

pages.text:
I took a slice of charcoal and sat down at the kitchen table, which was a cardboard box with a tablecloth over it.

I'm going to tell you my plan now, because I've never been good at keeping one to myself.

The plan was this. I was going to have the worst day of my life. I wasn't going to enjoy one single minute of it. I was going to sulk in the loudest, most obvious way possible, so that when the truck came and took everything I'd ever known to a place that was mostly cactus, everybody in my family would remember exactly how much they had ruined.

It seemed like a good plan. It was the only one I had.

It turned out to be the worst plan in the history of plans, and it is going to take me one hundred Saturdays to explain why. But I'm getting ahead of myself.

The toast, by the way, tasted like the inside of a chimney. I ate all of it, out of spite.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie sits scowling at a cardboard-box table with a plate of black toast, arms crossed, looking stubborn; behind him the bare kitchen with stacked boxes and Dad's fish apron on a hook.
